blocos.text: Quase toda análise agrupa por algum período: dia, semana, mês, trimestre. As funções de data são também onde os três bancos mais divergem, então este capítulo mostra cada operação nos três dialetos.
7.1. date_trunc: agrupando por período

`date_trunc` “arredonda para baixo” até o início do período. É a função certa para agrupar por mês ou semana, porque preserva a ordem cronológica e o ano: agrupar só por `extract(month ...)` misturaria janeiro de 2025 com janeiro de 2026.

blocos.titulo: Exercício 38 - Do segundo ao ano
blocos.code:
SELECT criado_em,
       date_trunc('hour', criado_em)    AS hora,
       date_trunc('day', criado_em)     AS dia,
       date_trunc('week', criado_em)    AS semana,      -- ❶
       date_trunc('month', criado_em)   AS mes,
       date_trunc('quarter', criado_em) AS trimestre,
       date_trunc('year', criado_em)    AS ano
FROM pedidos
WHERE id = 1;

SELECT date_trunc('quarter', criado_em)::date AS trimestre,      -- ❷
       count(*) AS pedidos,
       count(DISTINCT cliente_id) AS clientes
FROM pedidos
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
callouts: No Postgres, a semana começa na **segunda-feira** (padrão ISO). Em BigQuery, `WEEK` começa no domingo, e há `WEEK(MONDAY)` e `ISOWEEK`. Em Snowflake, depende do parâmetro de sessão `WEEK_START`.
O resultado de `date_trunc` sobre `timestamp` é outro `timestamp`; o `::date` deixa o rótulo mais limpo.

variantes.code:
SELECT criado_em,
       date_trunc('hour', criado_em) AS hora, date_trunc('day', criado_em) AS dia,
       date_trunc('week', criado_em) AS semana,          -- início da semana depende de WEEK_START
       date_trunc('month', criado_em) AS mes, date_trunc('quarter', criado_em) AS trimestre,
       date_trunc('year', criado_em) AS ano
FROM pedidos WHERE id = 1;

SELECT date_trunc('quarter', criado_em)::date AS trimestre, count(*) AS pedidos,
       count(DISTINCT cliente_id) AS clientes
FROM pedidos GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

SELECT criado_em,
       DATETIME_TRUNC(criado_em, HOUR) AS hora, DATETIME_TRUNC(criado_em, DAY) AS dia,
       DATETIME_TRUNC(criado_em, ISOWEEK) AS semana,     -- WEEK sozinho começa no domingo
       DATETIME_TRUNC(criado_em, MONTH) AS mes, DATETIME_TRUNC(criado_em, QUARTER) AS trimestre,
       DATETIME_TRUNC(criado_em, YEAR) AS ano
FROM loja.pedidos WHERE id = 1;

SELECT DATE_TRUNC(DATE(criado_em), QUARTER) AS trimestre, count(*) AS pedidos,
       count(DISTINCT cliente_id) AS clientes
FROM loja.pedidos GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

blocos.text: 7.2. extract e date_part: pegando uma parte da data

`extract(campo FROM valor)` é a forma padrão SQL; `date_part('campo', valor)` é a forma tradicional do Postgres. Use-as para **atributos** de uma data (dia da semana, hora do dia), e não para agrupar períodos.

blocos.titulo: Exercício 39 - Todas as partes de uma data
blocos.code:
SELECT criado_em,
       extract(year FROM criado_em)    AS ano,
       date_part('month', criado_em)   AS mes,              -- ❶
       extract(day FROM criado_em)     AS dia,
       extract(hour FROM criado_em)    AS hora,
       extract(dow FROM criado_em)     AS dia_semana_dom_0, -- ❷
       extract(isodow FROM criado_em)  AS dia_semana_iso,
       extract(week FROM criado_em)    AS semana_iso,
       extract(quarter FROM criado_em) AS trimestre,
       extract(doy FROM criado_em)     AS dia_do_ano,
       extract(epoch FROM criado_em)   AS segundos_desde_1970   -- ❸
FROM pedidos
WHERE id = 1;
callouts: `date_part` devolve `double precision`; `extract` devolve `numeric` (Postgres 14+). Para comparar com inteiros, tanto faz; para exibir, `extract` evita o `.0`.
`dow` vai de 0 (domingo) a 6; `isodow` vai de 1 (segunda) a 7 (domingo). Misturar as duas convenções é um erro clássico ao migrar relatórios entre bancos.
`epoch`: segundos desde 1970-01-01, útil para diferenças exatas e para integração com outros sistemas.

variantes.code:
SELECT criado_em,
       year(criado_em) AS ano, date_part('month', criado_em) AS mes, day(criado_em) AS dia,
       hour(criado_em) AS hora, dayofweek(criado_em) AS dia_semana_dom_0,
       dayofweekiso(criado_em) AS dia_semana_iso, weekiso(criado_em) AS semana_iso,
       quarter(criado_em) AS trimestre, dayofyear(criado_em) AS dia_do_ano,
       date_part(epoch_second, criado_em) AS segundos_desde_1970
FROM pedidos WHERE id = 1;

SELECT criado_em,
       EXTRACT(YEAR FROM criado_em) AS ano, EXTRACT(MONTH FROM criado_em) AS mes,
       EXTRACT(DAY FROM criado_em) AS dia, EXTRACT(HOUR FROM criado_em) AS hora,
       EXTRACT(DAYOFWEEK FROM criado_em) AS dia_semana_dom_1,   -- 1 = domingo, 7 = sábado
       EXTRACT(ISOWEEK FROM criado_em) AS semana_iso, EXTRACT(QUARTER FROM criado_em) AS trimestre,
       EXTRACT(DAYOFYEAR FROM criado_em) AS dia_do_ano,
       UNIX_SECONDS(TIMESTAMP(criado_em)) AS segundos_desde_1970
FROM loja.pedidos WHERE id = 1;

blocos.titulo: Exercício 40 - Mapa de calor: dia da semana × período do dia
blocos.code:
SELECT (ARRAY['seg', 'ter', 'qua', 'qui', 'sex', 'sáb', 'dom'])[extract(isodow FROM criado_em)::int] AS dia,   -- ❶
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE extract(hour FROM criado_em) < 12)                AS manha,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE extract(hour FROM criado_em) BETWEEN 12 AND 17)   AS tarde,
       count(*) FILTER (WHERE extract(hour FROM criado_em) >= 18)               AS noite,
       count(*) AS total
FROM pedidos
GROUP BY extract(isodow FROM criado_em)          -- ❷
ORDER BY extract(isodow FROM criado_em);
callouts: Um array literal indexado pelo dia ISO traduz o número em nome. No Postgres, arrays começam em 1.
Agrupar pela expressão numérica (e não pelo nome) mantém a ordem segunda → domingo no `ORDER BY`.

variantes.code:
SELECT decode(dayofweekiso(criado_em), 1, 'seg', 2, 'ter', 3, 'qua', 4, 'qui', 5, 'sex', 6, 'sáb', 7, 'dom') AS dia,
       count_if(hour(criado_em) < 12) AS manha,
       count_if(hour(criado_em) BETWEEN 12 AND 17) AS tarde,
       count_if(hour(criado_em) >= 18) AS noite,
       count(*) AS total
FROM pedidos
GROUP BY dayofweekiso(criado_em), dia
ORDER BY dayofweekiso(criado_em);

SELECT ['dom', 'seg', 'ter', 'qua', 'qui', 'sex', 'sáb'][OFFSET(EXTRACT(DAYOFWEEK FROM criado_em) - 1)] AS dia,
       countif(EXTRACT(HOUR FROM criado_em) < 12) AS manha,
       countif(EXTRACT(HOUR FROM criado_em) BETWEEN 12 AND 17) AS tarde,
       countif(EXTRACT(HOUR FROM criado_em) >= 18) AS noite,
       count(*) AS total
FROM loja.pedidos
GROUP BY EXTRACT(DAYOFWEEK FROM criado_em), dia
ORDER BY EXTRACT(DAYOFWEEK FROM criado_em);

blocos.text: 7.3. Aritmética de datas e intervalos

blocos.titulo: Exercício 41 - Somando, subtraindo e medindo
blocos.code:
SELECT current_date                                      AS hoje,
       current_date + 30                                 AS daqui_30_dias,          -- ❶
       current_date + interval '1 month'                 AS daqui_1_mes,
       date '2026-01-31' + interval '1 month'            AS fim_de_janeiro_mais_1_mes,   -- ❷
       date '2026-12-25' - date '2026-11-13'             AS dias_ate_o_natal,       -- ❸
       age(date '2026-11-13', date '1994-03-21')         AS idade,                  -- ❹
       extract(year FROM age(date '2026-11-13', date '1994-03-21')) AS anos_completos,
       (date_trunc('month', date '2026-02-10') + interval '1 month - 1 day')::date AS ultimo_dia_de_fevereiro;
callouts: `date + inteiro` soma dias e continua sendo `date`. Com `interval`, o resultado vira `timestamp`.
Somar um mês a 31 de janeiro dá 28 de fevereiro: o banco ajusta para o último dia válido.
`date - date` devolve um número inteiro de dias.

`age` devolve um intervalo “humano” (`32 years 7 mons 23 days`), ideal para idades. Cuidado com o `datediff(year, ...)` do Snowflake e o `DATE_DIFF(..., YEAR)` do BigQuery: eles contam **viradas de ano**, não anos completos.

variantes.code:
SELECT current_date AS hoje,
       dateadd(day, 30, current_date) AS daqui_30_dias,
       dateadd(month, 1, current_date) AS daqui_1_mes,
       dateadd(month, 1, '2026-01-31'::date) AS fim_de_janeiro_mais_1_mes,
       datediff(day, '2026-11-13'::date, '2026-12-25'::date) AS dias_ate_o_natal,
       datediff(year, '1994-03-21'::date, '2026-11-13'::date) AS diferenca_de_anos,   -- conta viradas de ano!
       last_day('2026-02-10'::date) AS ultimo_dia_de_fevereiro;

SELECT CURRENT_DATE() AS hoje,
       DATE_ADD(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 30 DAY) AS daqui_30_dias,
       DATE_ADD(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 1 MONTH) AS daqui_1_mes,
       DATE_ADD(DATE '2026-01-31', INTERVAL 1 MONTH) AS fim_de_janeiro_mais_1_mes,
       DATE_DIFF(DATE '2026-12-25', DATE '2026-11-13', DAY) AS dias_ate_o_natal,
       LAST_DAY(DATE '2026-02-10') AS ultimo_dia_de_fevereiro;

blocos.text: 7.4. Coortes: date_trunc com janelas

Uma análise de coorte agrupa clientes pelo mês da primeira compra e acompanha quantos voltam nos meses seguintes. É uma combinação direta de `date_trunc`, `min() OVER (PARTITION BY ...)` e agregação condicional.

blocos.titulo: Exercício 42 - Retenção por coorte mensal
blocos.code:
WITH base AS (
    SELECT cliente_id,
           date_trunc('month', criado_em)::date AS mes,
           min(date_trunc('month', criado_em)::date) OVER (PARTITION BY cliente_id) AS coorte   -- ❶
    FROM pedidos
    WHERE status <> 'cancelado'
)
SELECT coorte,
       count(DISTINCT cliente_id) FILTER (WHERE mes = coorte)                       AS clientes,   -- ❷
       count(DISTINCT cliente_id) FILTER (WHERE mes = coorte + interval '1 month')  AS mes_1,
       count(DISTINCT cliente_id) FILTER (WHERE mes = coorte + interval '2 months') AS mes_2,
       count(DISTINCT cliente_id) FILTER (WHERE mes = coorte + interval '3 months') AS mes_3
FROM base
WHERE coorte >= '2025-01-01' AND coorte < '2025-07-01'
GROUP BY coorte
ORDER BY coorte;
callouts: O menor mês de compra de cada cliente, repetido em todas as suas linhas: a coorte.

Para cada coorte, quantos clientes compraram no próprio mês, um, dois e três meses depois. Snowflake e BigQuery não têm `FILTER`, mas `count(DISTINCT IF(...))` faz o mesmo, porque `count` ignora NULLs.

variantes.code:
WITH base AS (
    SELECT cliente_id, date_trunc('month', criado_em)::date AS mes,
           min(date_trunc('month', criado_em)::date) OVER (PARTITION BY cliente_id) AS coorte
    FROM pedidos WHERE status <> 'cancelado'
)
SELECT coorte,
       count(DISTINCT iff(mes = coorte, cliente_id, NULL)) AS clientes,
       count(DISTINCT iff(mes = dateadd(month, 1, coorte), cliente_id, NULL)) AS mes_1,
       count(DISTINCT iff(mes = dateadd(month, 2, coorte), cliente_id, NULL)) AS mes_2,
       count(DISTINCT iff(mes = dateadd(month, 3, coorte), cliente_id, NULL)) AS mes_3
FROM base
WHERE coorte >= '2025-01-01' AND coorte < '2025-07-01'
GROUP BY coorte ORDER BY coorte;

WITH base AS (
    SELECT cliente_id, DATE_TRUNC(DATE(criado_em), MONTH) AS mes,
           min(DATE_TRUNC(DATE(criado_em), MONTH)) OVER (PARTITION BY cliente_id) AS coorte
    FROM loja.pedidos WHERE status <> 'cancelado'
)
SELECT coorte,
       count(DISTINCT IF(mes = coorte, cliente_id, NULL)) AS clientes,
       count(DISTINCT IF(mes = DATE_ADD(coorte, INTERVAL 1 MONTH), cliente_id, NULL)) AS mes_1,
       count(DISTINCT IF(mes = DATE_ADD(coorte, INTERVAL 2 MONTH), cliente_id, NULL)) AS mes_2,
       count(DISTINCT IF(mes = DATE_ADD(coorte, INTERVAL 3 MONTH), cliente_id, NULL)) AS mes_3
FROM base
WHERE coorte >= '2025-01-01' AND coorte < '2025-07-01'
GROUP BY coorte ORDER BY coorte;

blocos.text: 7.5. Fusos horários e formatação

blocos.titulo: Exercício 43 - Instantes, relógios e textos
blocos.code:
SELECT timestamptz '2026-11-13 15:00:00+00'                                AS instante_utc,          -- ❶
       timestamptz '2026-11-13 15:00:00+00' AT TIME ZONE 'America/Sao_Paulo' AS relogio_em_sp,       -- ❷
       timestamp '2026-11-13 12:00:00' AT TIME ZONE 'America/Sao_Paulo'     AS meio_dia_sp_como_instante,   -- ❸
       to_char(timestamp '2026-11-13 09:05:00', 'DD/MM/YYYY HH24:MI')       AS formatado,            -- ❹
       to_char(date '2026-11-13', 'YYYY-"T"Q')                              AS ano_trimestre,
       to_date('13/11/2026', 'DD/MM/YYYY')                                  AS de_texto_para_data;
callouts: `timestamptz` guarda um **instante** absoluto. Ele é exibido no fuso da sessão (no laboratório, UTC).
`AT TIME ZONE` sobre um instante devolve o **relógio de parede** naquele fuso: 12:00 em São Paulo.
O caminho inverso: um horário local de São Paulo convertido em instante.
`to_char` formata com máscaras (`DD`, `MM`, `YYYY`, `HH24`, `MI`). Texto literal na máscara vai entre aspas duplas.

       convert_timezone('America/Sao_Paulo', 'UTC', '2026-11-13 12:00:00'::timestamp_ntz) AS meio_dia_sp_em_utc,
       to_char('2026-11-13 09:05:00'::timestamp, 'DD/MM/YYYY HH24:MI') AS formatado,

       DATETIME(TIMESTAMP '2026-11-13 15:00:00+00', 'America/Sao_Paulo') AS relogio_em_sp,
       TIMESTAMP(DATETIME '2026-11-13 12:00:00', 'America/Sao_Paulo') AS meio_dia_sp_como_instante,

blocos.titulo: Desafio 8 - Trimestres de 2025 e participação no ano
blocos.enunciado: Para pedidos **não cancelados** de 2025, calcule o faturamento por trimestre (`trimestre` como `date`, obtido com `date_trunc`, e `faturamento`, soma de `quantidade * preco_unitario`) e a participação de cada trimestre no total do ano (`pct_ano`, em %, arredondada com 1 casa, usando `sum(...) OVER ()`). Ordene por `trimestre`.
blocos.inicial:
SELECT extract(quarter FROM p.criado_em) AS trimestre, count(*) AS pedidos
FROM pedidos p
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1;
blocos.solucao:
WITH trimestral AS (
    SELECT date_trunc('quarter', p.criado_em)::date AS trimestre,
           sum(i.quantidade * i.preco_unitario) AS faturamento
    FROM pedidos p
    JOIN itens_pedido i ON i.pedido_id = p.id
    WHERE p.status <> 'cancelado'
      AND p.criado_em >= '2025-01-01' AND p.criado_em < '2026-01-01'
    GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT trimestre, faturamento,
       round(100.0 * faturamento / sum(faturamento) OVER (), 1) AS pct_ano
FROM trimestral
ORDER BY trimestre;

blocos.text: This chapter is a full interview case, in the format it usually appears: a small schema, a sequence of questions that build **a single query** step by step, and traps hidden in the data.
8.1. Where the data lives

The marketplace tables live in their own schema, `marketplace`, next to the store tables in `public`. The database `search_path` includes both schemas, so `FROM creators` and `FROM marketplace.creators` reach the same table.

blocos.titulo: Exercise 44 - Finding the marketplace schema
blocos.code:
SHOW search_path;                                        -- ❶

SELECT table_schema, table_name                          -- ❷
FROM information_schema.tables
WHERE table_schema IN ('public', 'marketplace')
ORDER BY table_schema, table_name;

SELECT count(*) AS creators FROM marketplace.creators;   -- ❸
SELECT count(*) AS creators FROM creators;
callouts: The list of schemas Postgres searches, in order, when a table name is not qualified. It should show `public, marketplace`.
Every table in both schemas. In `psql`, `\dt marketplace.*` does the same.
Qualified and unqualified names return the same 6 creators. If a name existed in both schemas, the first schema in the `search_path` would win; qualify the name when in doubt.

blocos.text: The lab engine checks at startup whether the `marketplace` schema exists and loads it from `trails/sql/db/03_marketplace.sql` if it does not. Every dataset declared in `trails/sql/trail.json` is loaded the same way, so a database volume created earlier never misses a schema. To reset everything instead: `docker compose down -v` and then `docker compose up -d`.
8.2. The schema

rows: Two different creators are both named “Nova”.
A creator may have no samples (Kai).
No `creator_id`: the creator comes through the sample.

blocos.text: **How to work:** write each query from the schema alone, without looking at solutions, and say out loud, for every CTE and every window function, the **grain** (what one row is), the **partition** and the **order**. Run every step and check the row count.
8.3. Steps 1 to 4: the build-up (solved)

1. List the creators' names and countries. 2. Add the age of each creator's account in days, from the signup date. 3. Add the total number of license purchases per creator, keeping the earlier columns. 4. Add the total amount paid to each creator.

blocos.titulo: Exercise 45 - The query built in steps 1 to 4
blocos.code:
with creators_basis as (                       -- ❶
    select
        creator_id,
        name,
        country,
        current_date - signup_date as account_age_in_days    -- ❷
    from creators
),

total_purchases as (                           -- ❸
    select
        s.creator_id,
        count(l.license_id) as total_purchases
    from samples s
    left join licenses l
        on s.sample_id = l.sample_id
    group by s.creator_id
),

total_payouts as (
    select
        creator_id,
        sum(amount) as total_amount
    from creator_payouts
    where status = 'paid'                      -- ❹
    group by creator_id
)

select
    c.creator_id,
    c.name,
    c.country,
    c.account_age_in_days,
    coalesce(t.total_purchases, 0) as total_purchases,     -- ❺
    coalesce(p.total_amount, 0) as total_amount
from creators_basis c
left join total_purchases t
    on t.creator_id = c.creator_id
left join total_payouts p
    on c.creator_id = p.creator_id
order by c.creator_id;
callouts: Grain: one row per creator. `creators` drives the query, because every creator must survive.
`date - date` in Postgres returns an integer number of days.
Each fact is aggregated at creator grain in its own CTE and only then joined. This avoids the row multiplication (fan-out) you would get by joining licenses and payouts at the same time.

The status filter sits **inside** the aggregating CTE. License 1004 has a `failed` and a `paid` payout, so filtering avoids counting it twice. A `where` after the `left join` would cancel the outer join.
`coalesce` turns the NULLs created by the `left join` into 0 for creators without purchases or payouts.

blocos.text: Expected result (6 rows; the account age depends on today's date):
Lessons from the review

**The driving table goes on the left.** If every creator must survive, `creators` drives and each aggregated child attaches with a `left join`. The foreign keys point from child to parent, so a parent can have no children. You can decide this from the schema alone.
**Aggregate each fact at creator grain** in its own CTE, then join.
**`count(column)` ignores NULLs**, so a `left join` plus `count(l.license_id)` gives 0 for creators without purchases.
**`coalesce` only fires if an outer join sits above it.**
**Say your assumptions out loud**: “paid” means `status = 'paid'`; 0 vs NULL for creators with no payouts.
**Mechanical habit**: trailing commas before `from` were the most common error. Writing select lists with leading commas helps.
**Check the row count at every step**: 6 creators. If a step returns 4, a join is dropping creators.
8.4. Traps to think about before steps 5 to 14
**Postgres has no `qualify`.** Filtering on a window result needs a CTE or subquery (section 6.14).
**Partition key:** two creators are both named “Nova”. Partition by `creator_id`, never by `name`.
**Where the creator is:** licenses don't carry `creator_id`. You get it through samples, so think about whether that join can duplicate rows.
**Determinism:** a window `order by` on a non-unique column makes `row_number` and `lag` non-deterministic. Add a tie-breaker.
**Payouts have no date column.** Decide what defines “order” for step 14 and say it out loud.
**Date arithmetic:** `date - date` gives an integer, `timestamp - timestamp` gives an interval. Know which one you have at each step.
**Say it out loud:** “partition by creator, order by purchase date” for every window function.

Where `lag` fits in this dataset: days between a creator's consecutive purchases (the main use case), days from signup to first sale, month-over-month revenue change, and payout retries on the same license (license 1004 has two attempts).
8.5. Steps 5 to 14: practice without an answer key

Each step below has an editor connected to Postgres, but **no solution and no automatic check**: several questions require a decision from you, and that decision is what an interview evaluates. Use the self-check line to catch join mistakes, not to find the answer.
Part A: row_number and ranking

blocos.titulo: Step 5 - Number each creator's purchases
blocos.enunciado: For each creator, number their license purchases in chronological order. Make the numbering deterministic. Self-check: 8 rows (one per license); the numbers go up to 3 for creator 1 and up to 2 for creators 2 and 4.

blocos.titulo: Step 6 - First purchase only, and days after signup
blocos.enunciado: Keep only each creator's first purchase, and show how many days after signup it happened. Self-check: 4 rows if only creators with purchases appear; decide, and justify, whether Kai and Lea should appear.

blocos.titulo: Step 7 - Revenue rank within each country
blocos.enunciado: Rank creators by revenue within their country. Decide how ties should behave (`rank` vs `dense_rank`), and keep creators with no revenue. Self-check: 6 rows; the US has 3 creators and every other country has 1. Say which column you are calling “revenue”.

blocos.text: Part B: lag and lead

blocos.titulo: Step 8 - Days since the creator's previous purchase
blocos.enunciado: For each purchase, show the days since that creator's previous purchase. The first purchase has no previous one, so decide how to show that. Self-check: 8 rows; exactly 4 of them (one per creator with purchases) have no previous purchase.

blocos.titulo: Step 9 - Average gap between purchases, flag over 30 days
blocos.enunciado: Per creator, show the average gap between purchases, and flag creators whose average gap is over 30 days. Self-check: only 3 creators have at least two purchases (1, 2 and 4); decide what to show for creators with a single purchase.

blocos.titulo: Step 10 - Next purchase with lead
blocos.enunciado: For each purchase, also show the date of the creator's next purchase (`lead`), and the number of days until it. Self-check: 8 rows; each creator's last purchase (4 rows in total) has no next one.

blocos.text: Part C: running totals and frames

blocos.titulo: Step 11 - Running revenue and share of the creator's total
blocos.enunciado: Add a running revenue total per creator, ordered by purchase date, and each purchase's share of that creator's total revenue (`sum() over (partition by ...)` with no `order by`). Self-check: 8 rows; for each creator, the running total on the last purchase equals the total, and the shares add up to 100%.

blocos.titulo: Step 12 - Purchases in the trailing 30 days
blocos.enunciado: Count each creator's purchases in the trailing 30 days at every purchase, including the current one (a `range` frame with an interval). Self-check: 8 rows; no value can be below 1. Say out loud whether “30 days” includes the date exactly 30 days earlier.

blocos.text: Part D: dates and time series

blocos.titulo: Step 13 - Monthly revenue, change, and months with no sales
blocos.enunciado: Monthly revenue with the month-over-month change (`date_trunc` + `lag`). Then make months with no sales appear as 0 (`generate_series`). Self-check: every month from May to October 2026 already has sales, so the zero-fill only shows up if you extend the series; from May to November you should get 7 rows, with November at 0.

blocos.titulo: Step 14 - Payout attempts per license
blocos.enunciado: Per license, number the payout attempts in order, and flag licenses where the first attempt did not succeed. Payouts have no date: say what defines the order. Self-check: 8 payouts for 7 licenses; only one license has two attempts. Also note that one sold license has no payout at all: should it appear?

blocos.text: 8.6. Review of the PII redaction case (BigQuery)

A second interview case, in BigQuery, about user data synced by Fivetran: `raw_users` (one row per change, with `updated_at` and `_fivetran_synced`) and `erasure_requests` (`completed_at` is NULL while the request is open). The questions were: (1) the latest version of each user; (2) users with a completed erasure request who still have PII in `raw_users`; (3) how PII can arrive after completion; (4) rows that have PII when the previous row had none, with the days since the previous row.

rows: Filter out the row with a NULL `user_id`. Order by `updated_at desc, _fivetran_synced desc`: one user had three rows with the same `updated_at`, and without the tie-breaker the result changes between runs.

Check **all history rows**, not only the latest: old PII must be redacted too. A `count(*) as rows_with_pii` shows how many rows are left to redact; `distinct` over `(user_id, completed_at)` only collapses identical pairs. The join needs its `on`.
4. PII after a row with none

“Had none” means email **and** name are NULL. `lag()` returns NULL both when the previous row has no PII and when there is **no previous row** at all, so lag a boolean (or require a previous row to exist) to avoid false positives on each user's first row.
BigQuery uses `timestamp_diff(later, earlier, DAY)`, not `datediff('day', ...)`. `qualify` works in BigQuery and Snowflake, but not in Postgres.

blocos.text: The “latest row per key” pattern from question 1 is the same as in section 6.6. In Postgres, without `qualify`, use a CTE with `row_number()` or `DISTINCT ON`; with CDC data, always break ties with a second time column (here, `_fivetran_synced`).

capitulos.titulo: 9. SQL em produção: dbt e SQLMesh

blocos.text: Em projetos de dados, o SQL raramente vive solto num arquivo: ele é organizado em **modelos** versionados, testados e executados em ordem de dependência por uma ferramenta de transformação. As duas mais usadas hoje são o **dbt** e o **SQLMesh**. As duas partem do mesmo princípio (cada modelo é um `SELECT`, e a ferramenta cuida de criar tabelas ou views, da ordem de execução e dos testes), mas com sintaxes e filosofias diferentes. Este capítulo usa o marketplace do capítulo 8 como exemplo.
Os exemplos deste capítulo são para leitura: o laboratório executa SQL puro no Postgres, e os blocos com `{{ }}`, `{% %}`, `MODEL (...)` ou `@` só funcionam dentro de um projeto dbt ou SQLMesh.
9.1. dbt: modelos, ref e source

No dbt, cada arquivo `.sql` em `models/` é um modelo, e o nome do arquivo é o nome da tabela ou view criada. O SQL é processado pelo **Jinja** antes de ir para o banco: `{{ ... }}` insere valores e `{% ... %}` controla a lógica.

blocos.titulo: Exercício 46 - Fontes e um modelo de staging no dbt
blocos.code:
# models/staging/_sources.yml
version: 2
sources:
  - name: marketplace            # ❶
    schema: marketplace
    tables:
      - name: creators
      - name: samples
      - name: licenses
      - name: creator_payouts
callouts: `sources` declara as tabelas brutas que o projeto lê. `{{ source('marketplace', 'licenses') }}` vira `"marketplace"."licenses"` na compilação: o mesmo schema usado no laboratório.
`config` define como o modelo é materializado: `view`, `table`, `incremental` ou `ephemeral` (vira CTE dentro de quem o usa).
O staging resolve uma armadilha do capítulo 8 de uma vez: a licença ganha o `creator_id`, e os modelos seguintes não precisam repetir o join.

select

    s.creator_id,                          -- ❸

    l.price,
    l.purchase_date
from {{ source('marketplace', 'licenses') }} as l
join {{ source('marketplace', 'samples') }} as s
    on s.sample_id = l.sample_id

),

total_purchases as (

    from {{ ref('stg_licenses') }}               -- ❶

blocos.text: 9.2. dbt: testes e documentação em YAML

blocos.titulo: Exercício 48 - Testes de dados e teste unitário
blocos.code:
version: 2
models:
  - name: dim_creators
    description: Uma linha por criador, com compras e total pago.
    columns:
      - name: creator_id
        data_tests:                    # ❶ (tests: em versões anteriores ao 1.8)
          - unique
          - not_null
      - name: total_amount
        data_tests:
          - not_null

  - name: stg_licenses
    columns:
      - name: creator_id
        data_tests:
          - relationships:              # ❷
              to: source('marketplace', 'creators')
              field: creator_id

unit_tests:                             # ❸
  - name: total_pago_ignora_falhas
    model: dim_creators
    given:
      - input: source('marketplace', 'creators')
        rows:
          - {creator_id: 2, name: Ben Carter, country: US, signup_date: 2023-11-02}
      - input: ref('stg_licenses')
        rows:
          - {license_id: 1004, creator_id: 2}
      - input: source('marketplace', 'creator_payouts')
        rows:
          - {payout_id: 4, creator_id: 2, license_id: 1004, amount: 20, status: failed}
          - {payout_id: 5, creator_id: 2, license_id: 1004, amount: 20, status: paid}
    expect:

callouts: Testes genéricos prontos: `unique`, `not_null`, `accepted_values` e `relationships`. Cada teste vira uma consulta que procura linhas inválidas; se encontrar alguma, falha.
`relationships` confere a integridade referencial que os data warehouses não garantem.

Testes unitários (dbt 1.8+) rodam o modelo sobre dados de entrada fixos e comparam com a saída esperada. É preciso dar linhas para **todas** as entradas diretas do modelo; colunas omitidas ficam NULL, e o `expect` compara só as colunas listadas. Este teste reproduz a armadilha da licença 1004: uma tentativa falha e uma paga devem somar 20, e não 40.

`is_incremental()` é verdadeiro quando a tabela já existe e a execução não é `--full-refresh`.

blocos.text: 9.4. SQLMesh: o modelo declara a si mesmo

No SQLMesh, cada modelo começa com um bloco `MODEL (...)` que descreve nome, tipo de carga, grão e auditorias. Não há `ref()`: os modelos se referenciam pelo **nome completo**, e o SQLMesh descobre as dependências analisando o próprio SQL (ele usa o SQLGlot, um parser de SQL, o que também lhe dá linhagem por coluna e tradução entre dialetos).

blocos.titulo: Exercício 51 - O staging e a fato incremental no SQLMesh
blocos.code:
MODEL (
  name analytics.stg_licenses,
  kind VIEW                                          -- ❶
);

SELECT
  l.license_id,
  s.creator_id,
  l.price,
  l.purchase_date
FROM marketplace.licenses AS l
JOIN marketplace.samples AS s
  ON s.sample_id = l.sample_id
callouts: Tipos de modelo (`kind`): `VIEW`, `FULL` (recriado inteiro), `INCREMENTAL_BY_TIME_RANGE`, `INCREMENTAL_BY_UNIQUE_KEY`, `SCD_TYPE_2`, entre outros.
Na carga por intervalo de tempo, o SQLMesh controla quais intervalos já foram processados e preenche só os que faltam, inclusive buracos antigos.
`grain` documenta o grão do modelo: o mesmo “say it out loud” do capítulo 8, agora registrado no código.
Auditorias rodam junto com o modelo e bloqueiam a carga se falharem.
Referência direta pelo nome do modelo, sem `ref()`.
Macros do SQLMesh começam com `@`. `@start_ds` e `@end_ds` são substituídas pelo intervalo que está sendo processado.

variantes.code:
MODEL (
  name analytics.fct_licenses,
  kind INCREMENTAL_BY_TIME_RANGE (
    time_column purchase_date                        -- ❷
  ),
  start '2026-01-01',
  cron '@daily',
  grain license_id,                                  -- ❸
  audits (
    not_null(columns := (license_id, creator_id)),   -- ❹
    unique_values(columns := (license_id))
  )
);

SELECT
  license_id,
  creator_id,
  price,
  purchase_date
FROM analytics.stg_licenses                          -- ❺
WHERE purchase_date BETWEEN @start_ds AND @end_ds    -- ❻

$ sqlmesh plan              # promove para produção
$ sqlmesh audit             # roda as auditorias
$ sqlmesh test              # roda os testes unitários (YAML em tests/)
$ sqlmesh render analytics.fct_licenses   # mostra o SQL final, com as macros resolvidas

rows: Nome completo do modelo, direto no SQL
`{{ config(...) }}` no modelo ou em YAML
